title: Is There a Science of Writing?
author: Carl Hendrick
summary: Carl Hendrick examines whether a 'science of writing' comparable to the science of reading exists, concluding that it does—but is younger, more diffuse, and harder to translate into policy-ready slogans. Unlike the science of reading, which rests on a narrow biological fact (the brain must be explicitly taught to map letters to sounds), writing draws on multiple systems simultaneously: language, motor control, working memory, knowledge, and motivation. The strongest research findings concern instruction rather than acquisition—we know what kinds of teaching improve writing (supported by meta-analyses from Graham and Kim) but understand less about the developmental trajectory of writing the way we understand phonological awareness or orthographic mapping. Hendrick argues that the field is better described as a 'science of writing instruction' than as a basic science of how children acquire the skill. Writing also lacks the unifying theoretical anchor that powered reading policy: the Simple View of Reading was clear and reductive in a productive way; writing has no equivalent. The reason writing lags reading in policy influence is partly journalistic—no equivalent to Emily Hanford's 'Sold a Story' has yet carried writing research to a mainstream audience.
points: * The science of writing is real but younger and more diffuse than the science of reading, lacking the theoretical anchor (Simple View of Reading), political backing, or media-friendly slogans that drove the reading reform movement. * Writing research is more a science of writing instruction than a developmental science—we know what kinds of teaching improve writing, but less about how children acquire the underlying skill. * Unlike reading (which rests on one narrow biological fact), writing involves simultaneous management of transcription, syntax, domain knowledge, audience awareness, working memory, and self-regulation—a complexity that resists a single unifying framework. * Graham and Kim have repeatedly argued that the science of writing is inseparable from the science of reading—comprehension and composition develop together and cannot be fully understood in isolation. * The reason writing lags reading in policy is partly journalistic: no equivalent to Emily Hanford's 'Sold a Story' has yet carried writing research to a mainstream audience with the same political force.
quotes: Writing, by contrast, has been almost entirely absent from this conversation.

The honest answer is that if we are happy with the term science of reading (and 'science' here is admittedly doing a lot of heavy lifting), then there probably is a science of writing. However, it is younger, more diffuse, and harder to translate into the kind of media-friendly slogans that tends to travel well.

The science of writing is closer to a science of writing instruction than to a basic science of how children acquire the actual skill of writing. In other words, we are better gardeners of writing than we are biologists of it: we know what helps it grow without fully understanding the thing that is growing.

The science of reading rests on a relatively narrow biological fact, namely that the brain is just not built to read and must be taught to map letters to sounds. Writing however, has no equivalent single mechanism.

Writing has no equivalent in terms of clarity and may never have one, mainly because its the simultaneous orchestration of transcription, sentence-level syntax, discourse structure, domain knowledge, audience awareness and self-regulation, all of it held in working memory at once.
